pairs.answer: Here is a structure for the literature review chapter. Open with a short section that defines the problem and explains why approximate search matters for retrieval systems at scale. Then group the prior work into three strands: graph-based indexes such as HNSW and NSG, quantisation methods such as product quantisation and its variants, and disk-resident designs such as DiskANN and SPANN. For each strand, describe the core idea, the trade-off it makes between recall, latency and memory, and the open questions the later papers try to answer. End each strand with a paragraph that connects it to your own research question, so the reader sees why the chapter exists. After the three strands, add a short synthesis that names the gap your thesis fills. I have formatted the reference list at the end in APA 7th edition, the style you use, with DOIs where the publisher provides them. Two of the papers you mentioned are preprints, so check whether a peer-reviewed version has appeared before you submit. Keep the chapter to about twelve pages; examiners tend to skim longer reviews.

pairs.memory: Our production database runs on AWS in the eu-west-1 region
pairs.answer: The latency spikes in the dashboard line up with the nightly backup window, so the first suspect is I/O contention rather than the application. During a snapshot the volume's throughput is shared between the backup and the live queries, and the slow queries in the log are exactly the ones that scan large tables. There are three ways to reduce the impact. First, move the backup to a read replica so the primary never takes the snapshot load. Second, if the replica is not an option, switch the volume to provisioned IOPS for the window, which costs more but caps the contention. Third, look at the two reports that run at the same hour and schedule them later. Since your production database runs in AWS eu-west-1, create the read replica in the same region so replication lag stays under a second and you pay no cross-region transfer. After the change, compare the p99 latency for a week before and after; the spikes should drop from around 900 milliseconds to the normal 40 to 60.

pairs.memory: I am training for the Mumbai marathon in January
pairs.answer: A sore knee after long runs is common, and most of the time it comes from load rather than injury. Start by looking at the last four weeks: if your weekly distance rose by more than about ten percent a week, the knee is probably telling you that the tissues have not caught up. Cut the next week's volume by a third, keep one easy run and one short run with strides, and replace the long run with an hour on the bike. Strength work helps more than most runners expect: two sessions a week of split squats, step-downs and hip bridges protect the knee by taking load off it. Check your shoes too; pairs past about 700 kilometres lose much of their cushioning. With the Mumbai marathon in January, you still have time to back off for a week now without losing fitness, and a short break is far cheaper than a month out later. If the pain is sharp, swells, or stays the morning after a rest day, see a physiotherapist before running again.

pairs.answer: A strong research proposal answers four questions in the first page: what problem you will solve, why it matters now, why your approach will work, and why you are the right team to do it. Reviewers read dozens of applications, so put the answers in plain sentences before any technical detail. The aims should be few and testable; three aims with clear milestones read better than six vague ones. In the methods, describe the riskiest step first and say what you will do if it fails, because reviewers look for that. The budget should follow the work plan line by line, with each salary and piece of equipment tied to an aim. With the Wellcome Trust application due on 30 November, aim to have a complete draft by the middle of the month so colleagues have two weeks to read it and you have time for the institutional sign-off. Ask at least one reader from outside your field: if they cannot explain your aims back to you, the panel will struggle too.

pairs.memory: I prefer Python over R for data analysis
pairs.answer: To compare the two groups, start by checking the shape of the data rather than jumping to a test. Plot the distribution of the outcome in each group; with fewer than thirty observations per group and visible skew, a t-test can mislead. If the distributions look roughly normal and the variances are similar, Welch's t-test is a safe default because it does not assume equal variances. If they are skewed, use the Mann-Whitney U test, and report the median and interquartile range instead of the mean. Either way, report an effect size alongside the p-value: Cohen's d for the t-test, or the rank-biserial correlation for Mann-Whitney. Since you prefer Python, scipy.stats has both tests, ttest_ind with equal_var set to False and mannwhitneyu, and pingouin adds the effect sizes in one call. Finally, check whether any observations appear twice or come from the same participant, because repeated measures need a paired test instead. Write down which test you chose and why before you look at the result.

pairs.memory: Our team does code review on GitHub pull requests with two approvals required
pairs.answer: Splitting the refactor into smaller changes is the right call; a two-thousand-line diff rarely gets a careful review. Start with a change that only moves code without altering behaviour, such as extracting the parser into its own module, so reviewers can check it quickly by comparing before and after. Then introduce the new interface behind the old one, with tests that pin the current behaviour. Only in the third change switch the callers over, one subsystem at a time. Each step should leave the main branch working, so you can stop or ship at any point. Write a short note at the top of each description that explains where it sits in the sequence and what the reviewer should focus on. Because your team needs two approvals on every GitHub pull request, line up the two reviewers for the whole series at the start, so the same people see each step and do not have to rebuild the context. Expect the first change to take longest to review; the later ones go faster once the plan is understood.

pairs.memory: I am visiting Tokyo from 12 to 19 April
pairs.answer: Japan is easy to get around, but a little preparation saves a lot of time. Buy a Suica or Pasmo card at the airport; it works on almost every train, subway and bus in the big cities and in most convenience stores. The Japan Rail Pass is only worth it if you plan several long trips on the shinkansen, so price out your route first. Carry some cash: many small restaurants and temples still do not take cards. Download an offline map and a translation app, and note your hotel's address in Japanese to show taxi drivers. Since you are in Tokyo from 12 to 19 April, you will catch the end of the cherry blossom season, so visit Shinjuku Gyoen or the Meguro River early in the morning before the crowds arrive. Restaurants in popular areas fill up at seven in the evening; eating at six or after eight is much easier. Tipping is not expected anywhere and can cause confusion, so simply thank the staff.
